Transcriptions were read from the scan for this demo and are illustrative; replace them with the project's checked scholarly transcriptions and translations before publication. Text in [square brackets] lies outside the crop that was read and is supplied from the standard edition.

title.en: Complete Map of the Myriad Countries of the World

creator: Matteo Ricci 利瑪竇 (1552–1610), with Li Zhizao 李之藻; impression by Zhang Wentao 張文燾 of Qiantang

catalogue.repository: Library of Congress, Geography and Map Division
catalogue.extent: 6 woodblock-printed sheets, mounted as two halves of three sheets each
catalogue.digitised: IIIF Image API 2, 22,678 × 20,538 px and 22,499 × 20,335 px
catalogue.credit: Library of Congress, Geography and Map Division. Free to use and reuse.

description: The 1602 Kunyu wanguo quantu is the third and largest of the Chinese world maps that Matteo Ricci produced with Chinese collaborators, printed from woodblocks in Beijing. It places China near the centre of an oval projection, names the five continents in Chinese, and surrounds the map with prefaces, cosmological diagrams and explanatory essays. The Library of Congress digitised the copy exhibited there in 2010 as two halves of three sheets each. This demo treats those halves as two switchable views, exactly as a map's front and back would be, and opens on the right half where a Chinese reader begins.

text.translation: Complete map of the myriad countries of the earth.
text.commentary: The six large characters sit in the upper right corner of the right-most sheet, where a Chinese reader begins. 坤輿 (kunyu, 'the earth as bearer') is a classical term for the terrestrial world; 萬國 ('ten thousand countries') announces the map's claim to completeness. The title is the natural first stop of any guided tour.
source: Library of Congress, item 2010585650, right half (ex000006Zb).
Huang Shijian 黃時鑒 and Gong Yingyan 龔纓晏, 利瑪竇世界地圖研究 (Shanghai: Shanghai guji, 2004) — starting point for the map's editions and texts.

text.original:
九重天圖
第一重月輪天　第二重辰星即水星天　第三重太白即金星天　第四重日輪天　第五重熒惑即火星天　第六重歲星即木星天　第七重填星即土星天　第八重二十八宿天　第九重宗動天
text.translation: Diagram of the Nine Heavens. First sphere: the heaven of the moon's disc; second: Chenxing, that is Mercury; third: Taibai, that is Venus; fourth: the heaven of the sun's disc; fifth: Yinghuo, that is Mars; sixth: Suixing, that is Jupiter; seventh: Tianxing, that is Saturn; eighth: the heaven of the twenty-eight lunar lodges; ninth: the Prime Mover.
text.commentary: A concentric diagram of the Aristotelian–Ptolemaic cosmos, with the earth (土 and 水) at the centre surrounded by the spheres of air and fire, then the planetary heavens. The ring inscriptions give each heaven's period of revolution. Ricci paired each classical Chinese planet name with the astronomical one (e.g. 太白 = 金星, Venus). Only the sphere names are transcribed here; the period figures are omitted.
source: Library of Congress, item 2010585650, right half, upper right corner.

text.original: ……輿地為五大州：曰歐邏巴，曰利未亞，曰亞細亞，曰[南北亞墨利加，曰墨瓦蠟泥加]……
text.translation: … The lands of the earth form five great continents: called Europe (Ouluoba), Libya (Liweiya, i.e. Africa), Asia (Yaxiya), [North and South America (Nanbei Yamolijia), and Magellanica (Mowalanijia)] …
text.commentary: Part of Ricci's own preface, which runs down the right margin of the right-most sheet. The passage shown is where the five continents are named in Chinese transliteration; the two names in brackets fall just below the crop that was read for this demo. The preface also explains the graticule, the antipodes and why the earth is round — the kind of text a reading panel should present column by column, with the original beside the translation.
source: Library of Congress, item 2010585650, right half, right margin.
John D. Day, 'The Search for the Origins of the Chinese Manuscript of Matteo Ricci's Maps', Imago Mundi 47 (1995) — on the map's textual tradition.

text.translation: Instrument of heaven and earth (armillary sphere).
text.commentary: In the lower right corner a small terrestrial globe sits at the centre of the celestial sphere. The oblique band is the ecliptic, divided by the twenty-four solar terms (清明, 穀雨, 立夏, 小滿 … are legible), so the diagram doubles as a calendar. Together with the Nine Heavens above it, it frames the map with the cosmology that justified Ricci's geography.
source: Library of Congress, item 2010585650, right half, lower right corner.

text.commentary: The sea off Zhejiang and Fujian is named for the ruling dynasty, as the map names China itself 大明 (Great Ming). Nearby labels give 南京, 浙江, 福建, 杭州 and the Ryukyu and Taiwan islands. A toponym annotation like this one is the simplest kind: a short label, its reading, and a note.
source: Library of Congress, item 2010585650, left half, right-most sheet.

text.original: 日本乃海內一大島，長三千二百里，寬不過六百里。今有六十六州，各有國主。俗尚強力，雖有總王而權常在強臣。其民多習武，少習文；土產銀、鐵、好漆。其王生子年三十，以王讓之。其國大抵不重寶石，只重金銀及古窯器。
text.translation: Japan is a great island within the sea, 3,200 li long and no more than 600 li wide. It now has sixty-six provinces, each with its own lord. Custom esteems strength: although there is a supreme king, power always lies with the strong ministers. Its people mostly practise arms and rarely letters; the land produces silver, iron and fine lacquer. When the king's son reaches thirty, the king yields the throne to him. On the whole the country does not value precious stones, only gold, silver and old kiln wares.
text.commentary: Ricci's note on Japan is printed in the sea beside the islands, whose provinces (常陸, 武藏, 陸奧 …) are named individually. The passage reads as reportage from Jesuit letters: the sixty-six provinces, the powerless emperor, the warrior culture, the taste for antique ceramics. Showing the note next to the place it describes is exactly what an annotation layer is for.
source: Library of Congress, item 2010585650, left half, right-most sheet, east of Japan.

text.commentary: Ricci divided the Pacific into a Lesser Eastern Ocean off Japan and a Greater Eastern Ocean (大東洋) towards the Americas, mirroring 小西洋 and 大西洋 on the other side of the world. The names were adopted into later Chinese geographical writing.
source: Library of Congress, item 2010585650, left half, right edge.

label.zh: 論地球比九重天之星遠且大幾何
label.en: Essay: how far and how large the earth is compared with the stars

text.original:
論地球比九重天之星遠且大幾何
余嘗留心於量天地法，且從大西庠天文諸士討論已[久]……自地心至第一重謂月天，四十八萬……第三重謂太白即金星天，二百四十……第六重謂歲星即木星天，一萬二千……
text.translation: On how far and how large the earth is compared with the stars of the nine heavens. I have long paid attention to the methods of measuring heaven and earth, and have discussed them with the astronomers of the great Western academies … From the centre of the earth to the first heaven, that of the moon, is 480,000 [li] … to the third, Venus, 2,40- … to the sixth, Jupiter, 12,000 … [distances continue for each sphere].
text.commentary: A long essay in the left margin, signed in Ricci's voice (余, 'I'), giving the distances of the planetary spheres and the sizes of the heavenly bodies in li. It is the textual companion of the Nine Heavens diagram on the opposite sheet. Only the title and opening are transcribed here; a full edition would present the columns one by one.
source: Library of Congress, item 2010585650, left half, left margin.

text.original:
錢塘張文燾過紙
萬曆壬寅孟秋日
text.translation: Impression taken by Zhang Wentao of Qiantang. A day in the first month of autumn of the renyin year of Wanli [1602].
text.commentary: The only date on the map. 過紙 ('passing the paper') is the printer's term for pulling an impression from the blocks; Qiantang is Hangzhou. The two short columns are easy to miss beside the essay, which is why a numbered index of annotations helps a reader find them.
source: Library of Congress, item 2010585650, left half, lower left.

text.translation: Map of the hemisphere south of the equator.
text.commentary: One of two polar hemispheres in the corners of the left half (its northern twin is in the upper left corner). A note beside them explains that these small maps follow 'a different form but the same principle' as the large one, and are easier to read for the regions near the poles.
source: Library of Congress, item 2010585650, left half, lower left corner.

text.original:
看北極法
用平圓版一面，或銅或木，務要平整愈佳。中掛一線，線端墜一丸子，以取其直。中心畫十字線，此直線即天頂也，橫線即地平也。此線以上為地上……
text.translation: Method for sighting the North Pole. Take one flat circular plate, of copper or of wood; it must be level, the flatter the better. Hang a thread from the middle with a small ball at its end, to obtain the vertical. Draw a cross through the centre: the vertical line is the zenith, the horizontal line is the horizon. Above this line is 'above the ground' …
text.commentary: Instructions for building a simple altitude instrument (a quadrant on a disc, with a plumb line and two sighting holes) so that a reader can measure the pole star's altitude and hence their own latitude. Ricci uses the map to teach method as well as geography. The device sits inside a circle in the ocean south of Australia's imagined coast.
source: Library of Congress, item 2010585650, left half, lower right.

title.zh: 六幅之間：讀利瑪竇的世界
title.en: Reading Ricci's world across six sheets

story.byline: Demo narrative. The text is illustrative and written for this prototype.

body: Printed in Beijing in 1602, the Kunyu wanguo quantu is nearly four metres wide. The Library of Congress scanned it as two halves of three sheets; the viewer on the right shows the right half, where a Chinese reader begins.
Scroll down. Each section flies the map to the place it discusses, the way the Leventhal 'Map Chat' pages swap detail images, but with the whole map staying zoomable underneath.
Six characters in the upper right corner name the map. 坤輿 is the earth as bearer of all things; 萬國 is the ten thousand countries it carries.
Before the geography comes the cosmology. The concentric diagram sets the earth at the centre of nine revolving heavens, each labelled with its planet in both classical and astronomical names.

Ricci's preface runs down the right margin. Here he names the five continents in Chinese transliteration, three of which are visible in this crop; the reading panel in the viewer shows the original beside the translation.
We switch to the left half of the map. The sea off Zhejiang and Fujian takes the dynasty's name, and the coast is dense with provincial labels.
Beside the Japanese islands Ricci prints a short report: sixty-six provinces, a powerless emperor, a warrior people, and a taste for old ceramics rather than jewels.

heading.zh: 論地球比九重天之星遠且大幾何

body: The left margin carries a long essay in Ricci's own voice giving the distances of the planetary spheres in li. It is the textual companion of the Nine Heavens diagram on the other sheet.
Two short columns record who pulled the impression and when: Zhang Wentao of Qiantang, in the first month of autumn, 1602.
The corners hold polar hemispheres drawn 'in a different form but by the same principle'. The tour ends here; open the viewer to explore the remaining annotations or to add your own.
